strengths: FreeKV addresses a practical bottleneck in offloaded KV retrieval with a coherent combination of speculative retrieval, selective correction, hybrid memory layouts, and double buffering.
The reported efficiency gains are substantial: up to 13.7× over ArkVale and 8.4× over ShadowKV. Figure 8 usefully separates the contributions of layout changes, buffering, and speculative retrieval.

Accuracy evaluation covers six models across long-input, long-generation, and reasoning tasks. FreeKV generally approaches full-cache accuracy and performs favorably against several relevant compression methods.
weaknesses: The central correction mechanism is insufficiently validated. There are no accuracy ablations comparing reuse without correction, selective correction, and current-query retrieval; no threshold sweep; and no correction-frequency measurements. High query cosine similarity does not necessarily imply stable selected pages, and averaging similarity across heads can conceal individual-head changes. The effectiveness and cost of this proxy need direct evidence.

The claimed fixed O(B) GPU memory usage is inconsistent with the implementation description. GPU-resident page summaries require O(L/p) storage, and retaining an uncompressed first layer introduces an additional context-dependent term. No measured memory-scaling results resolve this discrepancy.

Baseline modifications complicate interpretation. Quest and RaaS receive altered group-consistent selection, while ShadowKV receives periodic SVD updates for long generation. Their accuracy and runtime relative to the original implementations are not established. Since layout optimization accounts for most of the speedup, comparisons against baselines equipped with comparable transfer optimizations would better isolate FreeKV's algorithmic contribution.

Efficiency evaluation is limited to two 7–8B models, one A100 configuration, batch sizes up to four, and two fixed workload shapes. It omits full-cache and Quest timing where feasible, reasoning-model timing, context-length scaling, and latency breakdowns showing achieved overlap. Consequently, the broad efficiency and scalability claims exceed the demonstrated scope.

Near-lossless reasoning accuracy is not statistically established. MATH500 and GPQA use only 50 problems each, with no subset-selection details or confidence intervals. Eight samples per problem help assess sampling variation but do not replace broader problem coverage. Some differences are meaningful enough to investigate, including the 3.74-point AIME24 average-accuracy decrease for DeepSeek-R1-Qwen-7B.

Reproducibility and positioning need strengthening: software versions, kernel and transfer implementation details, benchmark sample counts, and threshold-selection procedures are incompletely specified. The distinction from prior temporal KV-sharing and attention-prediction methods is also underdeveloped. Overall, the promising system results are offset by unresolved validation and accounting issues.

strengths: Addresses an important inference bottleneck: selecting and transferring offloaded KV states can dominate decoding latency even when attention is sparse.

Presents a coherent algorithm–system design combining previous-step retrieval, selective correction, transfer-friendly CPU layouts, and double buffering. The layout and scheduling mechanisms are explained clearly.

Reports substantial measured improvements over ArkVale and ShadowKV. Figure 8 provides useful component-level timing ablations, including an additional benefit from speculative retrieval after layout optimizations.

Evaluates accuracy across six model variants and long-input, long-generation, and reasoning tasks. FreeKV generally remains close to full-cache accuracy and avoids several large degradations observed with competing methods.
weaknesses: The central correction mechanism lacks direct validation. There are no accuracy ablations comparing synchronous retrieval, uncorrected reuse, and corrected reuse; no threshold sweep; and no correction-frequency or missed-important-page measurements. High query cosine similarity does not establish stable selected pages, especially after averaging across heads. Consequently, the experiments do not establish when the proposed heuristic is reliable or its accuracy–latency trade-off.

The fixed O(B) GPU-memory claim in Table 1 and Section 2 is inconsistent with the described implementation. Section 4.1 retains page summaries on GPU, requiring storage proportional to the number of context pages, and Section 5.1 leaves the first layer uncompressed. Total GPU memory therefore retains context-dependent terms. No measured memory-scaling results substantiate the claimed capacity advantage.

Baseline modifications complicate interpretation. Quest and RaaS receive maximum-pooled group-consistent selection, whereas FreeKV uses softmax-based mean pooling; ShadowKV is modified to recompute SVD during generation. These changes can materially affect accuracy and latency, but comparisons with original implementations and ablations of the modifications are absent. The long-generation speedups therefore require more careful qualification.

The efficiency evaluation is narrow: one A100/PCIe configuration, two 7–8B models, batch sizes up to four, and two fixed input/output-length settings. Figure 7 omits full-cache and Quest latency where they fit, and no reasoning-model timing is reported. This leaves practical competitiveness against resident inference and applicability to the accuracy-tested reasoning workloads unresolved.

Most of the reported acceleration comes from hybrid layouts, which alone deliver up to 10.5× speedup. This is a useful engineering result, but the paper does not test whether existing retrieval methods equipped with the same transfer optimizations achieve comparable performance. Such a comparison is important for establishing the incremental value of the proposed retrieval algorithm.

The near-lossless accuracy claim is stronger than the statistical evidence. Reasoning evaluation uses only 50 MATH500 problems, 50 GPQA problems, and 30 AIME24 problems, without confidence intervals or a documented subset-selection procedure. Eight generations per problem help but do not resolve uncertainty across problems. For example, DeepSeek-R1-Qwen-7B AIME24 average accuracy decreases from 56.66 to 52.92.

Reproducibility and reporting need improvement: baseline implementation versions, timing boundaries, correction overhead, and cache-management details are insufficiently specified. Table 2 also reports identical Llama LongGenBench CR and Acc for Quest and FreeKV but different products; Table 3 reports 65.33% AIME24 pass@8, which is incompatible with the stated 30-problem, eight-sample protocol unless additional averaging was performed. These discrepancies require clarification.

strengths: FreeKV addresses an important inference bottleneck with a coherent combination of speculative retrieval, head-wise correction, hybrid CPU/GPU layouts, and double-buffered transfers. The scheduling and data-layout designs are clearly explained.

The reported efficiency gains are substantial: up to 13.7× over ArkVale and 8.4× over ShadowKV. Figure 8 usefully separates the contributions of layout optimization, double buffering, and speculative retrieval, including additional gains after the layout bottleneck is removed.

Accuracy evaluation spans long-input, long-generation, and reasoning tasks across six model variants. FreeKV generally remains close to full-cache performance and compares favorably with the evaluated compression methods.
weaknesses: The central algorithmic mechanism lacks adequate validation. There are no accuracy ablations separating speculative reuse, selective correction, and softmax-based group pooling; no threshold sweep; and no correction-frequency measurements. High query cosine similarity alone does not establish stable selected pages or attention outputs, particularly after averaging across heads. The paper should measure retrieval overlap and missed attention mass and compare against synchronous retrieval using the same selection rule.

The fixed O(B) GPU-memory claim in Table 1 and Section 2 is incorrect for the described implementation. GPU-resident page summaries grow with context length, contributing O(L/p) storage for fixed head dimensions. The uncompressed first layer adds another context-dependent component whose placement is insufficiently specified. Actual peak-memory measurements and corrected complexity accounting are needed.

Baseline modifications complicate interpretation. Quest and RaaS receive maximum-pooled group selection, whereas FreeKV uses softmax-based mean pooling; ShadowKV is extended with periodic SVD recomputation. These changes can affect both accuracy and runtime, but their effects are not isolated. Since hybrid layouts deliver most of the speedup, applying equivalent transfer optimizations to competing retrieval systems would help establish the contribution beyond implementation differences.

The evidence for 'near-lossless' accuracy is insufficiently quantified. MATH500 and GPQA use only 50 problems each, with no disclosed subset-selection procedure or uncertainty estimates. Eight samples per problem do not eliminate uncertainty from the small problem set. Some average-accuracy decreases are nontrivial, such as 56.66 to 52.92 on AIME24 for DeepSeek-R1-Qwen-7B. Statistical comparisons are needed to distinguish preservation from sampling variability.

Efficiency and reproducibility coverage remain limited: one GPU configuration, two 7–8B models, batch sizes up to four, and a single cache budget. There is no full-cache performance baseline where feasible, no measured memory scaling, and no efficiency evaluation of the reasoning models central to the motivation. Software versions, implementation availability, timing methodology, and detailed cache-management policies are also missing. These gaps leave a promising systems contribution slightly below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: Addresses an important inference bottleneck with a coherent combination of previous-step KV retrieval, selective correction, contiguous CPU layouts, and double-buffered transfers.

Reports substantial end-to-end improvements over several retrieval baselines across two models and multiple batch sizes. Figure 9 usefully separates the contributions of layout optimization, buffering, and speculative retrieval.

Accuracy evaluation covers long-input, long-generation, and reasoning tasks across six model variants. Threshold and selection ablations provide useful evidence that correction improves on unconditional reuse.
weaknesses: Baseline modifications materially complicate the comparisons. Appendix A changes Quest, RaaS, and InfiniGen to group-consistent maximum pooling, while FreeKV uses its preferred softmax-mean pooling; ShadowKV additionally receives periodic SVD recomputation. Results against original implementations and controlled variants are needed to distinguish algorithmic gains from modification effects. Figure 9 attributes most acceleration to layout changes, making comparisons against baselines equipped with the same transfer optimizations particularly important.

The fixed O(B) GPU-memory claim is incorrect as stated. Section 4.1 retains page summaries on GPU, whose storage grows with the number of context pages, giving an additional O(L/p) term when architectural dimensions are suppressed. Appendix A also leaves the first layer uncompressed. No measured memory scaling is provided to resolve these omissions.

The efficiency evidence does not establish the claimed accuracy–latency trade-off on difficult reasoning workloads. Timing covers only the general 7B/8B models, whereas Table 9 reports correction rates reaching 52% on reasoning tasks. Corrections put selection and recall back on the critical path, so general claims of full latency hiding require measured breakdowns and reasoning-model latency results.

Near-lossless accuracy is not firmly established statistically. MATH500 and GPQA use only 50 selected problems each, without a documented selection procedure or confidence intervals. Eight generations per problem do not replace broader problem coverage. Some losses are appreciable, including DeepSeek-R1-Qwen-7B AIME24 average accuracy falling from 56.66 to 52.92. Evaluation uses one retrieval budget, and LongBench v2 inputs are truncated to 64K.

The correction mechanism is only indirectly validated. High query cosine similarity does not itself establish stable retrieved pages or preserved attention mass, particularly after averaging across heads. The paper lacks direct measurements of missed attention mass, retrieval overlap, and correction false negatives, as well as a joint threshold-versus-latency evaluation.

There are concrete inconsistencies in the supporting evidence. Appendix B.3 claims maximum pooling of similarity triggers more corrections than mean pooling, contrary to the stated rule C < τ. Figures 16 and 18 appear to reproduce identical histograms and per-layer averages while labeling different models; the Llama figure also shows only 28 layers. These require correction before the supporting analyses can be trusted.

Practical comparisons remain incomplete: the main latency evaluation omits full-KV inference and excludes Quest even in configurations where it fits. Measurements on one A100 platform, without detailed transfer bandwidth, cache-hit rates, or timing variability, leave the deployment advantage and reproducibility insufficiently established.

strengths: FreeKV addresses an important practical bottleneck: CPU–GPU KV retrieval can dominate decoding latency even when sparse attention reduces computation.

The combination of previous-step retrieval, selective correction, hybrid memory layouts, and double buffering is coherent. Figure 9 provides useful component ablations, showing substantial gains from layout optimization and additional gains from speculative retrieval.

The evaluation spans long-input, long-generation, and reasoning tasks across several models. Reported accuracy is often close to full-cache inference, and the measured speedups over the evaluated offloading implementations are substantial.
The appendices provide useful implementation settings, threshold ablations, and correction-rate measurements rather than relying exclusively on aggregate results.
weaknesses: The claimed fixed O(B) GPU memory usage is incorrect for the described system. Section 4.1 retains page summaries on GPU, which require storage growing with context length, and Appendix A leaves the first layer uncompressed. Table 1 therefore omits context-dependent memory costs. Measured peak GPU and CPU memory across context lengths are needed to substantiate the scalability comparison.

Baseline modifications complicate attribution of the gains. Appendix A changes Quest, RaaS, and InfiniGen to use group-consistent maximum pooling, while FreeKV uses a separately evaluated softmax-mean strategy; ShadowKV is modified to periodically recompute SVD. These changes can affect both accuracy and runtime, but their effects relative to the original implementations are not isolated. Appendix B.1 also replaces InfiniGen's re-projection with the previous layer's query, so that ablation does not establish superiority over InfiniGen's actual prediction mechanism.

The efficiency evaluation does not sufficiently establish the claimed accuracy–efficiency frontier. It omits full-cache inference and excludes Quest even in configurations where it fits, evaluates only one GPU platform and two small models, and largely fixes the cache budget at 2048. Figure 9 shows that layout changes account for most of the improvement; applying comparable transfer optimizations to competing retrieval methods would help establish the distinctive benefit of FreeKV.

The near-lossless accuracy claim is stronger than the statistical evidence. MATH500 and GPQA use only 50 selected problems each, without a documented selection procedure or confidence intervals. Eight generations per problem do not substitute for broader problem coverage. Some losses are nontrivial, including DeepSeek-R1-Qwen-7B AIME24 avg@8 falling from 56.66 to 52.92. LongBench v2 inputs are also truncated to 64K, limiting conclusions about longer contexts.

Cosine similarity is motivated empirically but is not directly validated as a reliable detector of harmful retrieval changes. High query similarity need not preserve selected pages or attention outputs, particularly after averaging across heads. The paper should measure missed important pages or attention error conditional on the correction decision. Moreover, Table 9 reports correction rates reaching 52% on reasoning tasks, yet runtime measurements use general instruction models rather than these demanding reasoning workloads; full latency hiding is consequently not established across the claimed scenarios.

There are concrete reporting inconsistencies. Appendix B.3 says maximum pooling of cosine similarities triggers more corrections than mean pooling, although the stated rule C < τ implies the opposite for the same similarities. Figure 18, labeled Llama-3.1-8B, shows 28 layers and reproduces the per-layer averages of the Qwen figure. These issues require correction before the supporting analyses can be trusted.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: the manuscript's code-availability statement supplies no usable link, and important details such as benchmark subset identifiers, timing repetitions, software versions, and cache-management policies are insufficiently documented. Overall, the promising engineering contribution is outweighed by unresolved comparison, scalability, and evidence issues.

strengths: FreeKV addresses an important inference bottleneck with a coherent combination of previous-step retrieval, selective correction, hybrid memory layouts, and double buffering. The training-free design has practical relevance.
Reported efficiency gains are substantial: up to 13.7× over ArkVale and 8.4× over ShadowKV. Figure 9 usefully separates the contributions of memory layout, streamed recall, and speculation.

Accuracy evaluation covers long-input understanding, long generation, and reasoning across six model variants. Results generally remain close to full-cache inference, and the appendices provide useful selection, correction-threshold, and query-similarity analyses.
weaknesses: The claimed fixed O(B) GPU memory usage is incorrect for the described system. GPU-resident page summaries scale with context length, and Appendix A leaves the first layer uncompressed. Actual peak-memory measurements and a complete accounting of summaries, retained caches, and transfer buffers are needed to substantiate scalability.

Baseline modifications complicate attribution. Appendix A changes Quest, RaaS, and InfiniGen to group-consistent selection and periodically recomputes ShadowKV’s SVD. Original-versus-modified results are not provided. Since hybrid layouts alone produce up to 10.5× speedup, comparisons against retrieval baselines using equally optimized transfers would better establish the incremental contribution.

Efficiency is evaluated on one A100 configuration and two general-purpose models, without timing the reasoning workloads central to the motivation. Table 9 reports correction rates as high as 0.52 on reasoning tasks, potentially exposing considerable selection and recall latency. Full-cache and Quest timings should also be included wherever they fit in memory.

The near-lossless accuracy claim needs stronger statistical support. MATH500 and GPQA use only 50 problems each, with no confidence intervals or explained subset-selection procedure. Eight generations per problem do not replace broader problem coverage. Some losses are nontrivial: DeepSeek-R1-Qwen-7B AIME24 average accuracy falls from 56.66 to 52.92.

Cosine similarity is a plausible correction heuristic, but the paper does not directly establish how reliably it predicts retrieval-set changes or attention-output error. Budget and page-size sensitivity are also missing, limiting evidence beyond the single 2048-token, 32-token-page configuration.

Several reporting inconsistencies require resolution. Appendix B.3 says max pooling triggers more corrections, although correction occurs below the threshold and max similarity is at least mean similarity for identical queries. Figures 16 and 18 appear to duplicate the same 28-layer correction distributions while naming different models. The abstract announces available code but supplies no usable link. These issues reduce confidence in reproducibility and the supporting analysis.
